title: From Signal to PR: Anatomy of a Self-Improving Agent — Jason Lopatecki, Arize

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 73%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Arize builds developer platforms and tools (AX, Phoenix, Signal) for AI observability and agent operations. The talk is about the substrate other engineers use to build, monitor, and fix AI systems, including open-box customization of harnesses, sandboxes, and skills.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The system automates production incident response, debugging workflows, and issue investigation in enterprise environments. The inverted loop moves humans from responder to reviewer in enterprise ops contexts, and VPC deployment targets enterprise customers like Uber and Booking.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The system uses coding agents (Claude Code) to produce code fixes and PRs from production traces. The filesystem-based approach is designed specifically for coding agents to consume, positioning it partially in the coding assistant space.

summary: Jason Lopatecki, co-founder and CEO of Arize AI, presents 'From Signal to PR: Anatomy of a Self-Improving Agent' at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. He traces the evolution of Arize's in-product agent Alyx, candidly admitting the first version 'sucked' two years ago, and introduces Signal, the next-generation automation system built from those lessons. The core thesis is that observability is transforming from human-facing dashboards into telemetry that coding agents consume to autonomously diagnose and fix software. The key technical unlock is pulling production traces and logs as temp files directly into the code repository, because coding harnesses like Claude Code work well with files but poorly with dashboards. Arize inverts the debugging loop: instead of a human grabbing a ticket and investigating, the agent pre-investigates errors using composable skills that connect to observability platforms, gathering evidence and producing fixes or filing issues with attached traces before a human even looks. Lopatecki argues teams should trace and log ten times more than today because that telemetry reveals the exact code path software took, enabling agents to produce real fixes rather than guesses. He demonstrates a real example where Alyx hit a stream-canceled bug and Signal produced a one-to-two-line fix, while noting that larger fixes still require human involvement. The system is open-box: users choose their harness, sandbox, prompts, and skills. Arize installs in customer VPCs because enterprise customers like Uber and Booking will not connect production systems to external model providers. The product lineup includes AX (SaaS/VPC), Phoenix (open source), and Signal. In Q&A, Lopatecki explains that simply pointing Claude Code at data does not work without well-designed skills, and describes online evals as AI-judged assessments layered onto production traces that can catch recurring failures automatically.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a cohesive architecture for autonomous software improvement. The inverted debugging loop restructures incident response by having agents investigate first, which depends on the traces-on-filesystem approach to make observability data consumable by coding agents. Composable skills provide the abstraction layer that bridges observability platforms and agent harnesses, while the agent improvement loop ties investigation, fix proposal, and evaluation into a continuous cycle. The AI concepts—agent-consumed observability, self-improving systems, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluations—define the intelligence layer, while OpenInference standardization and 10x tracing investment provide the data substrate. Together, these concepts describe a paradigm shift where observability infrastructure is no longer built for humans reading dashboards but for agents autonomously diagnosing, fixing, and learning from production failures. The practical constraints—VPC deployment for enterprise security, sandboxed execution, and swarm management—ensure this architecture can operate in real production environments.
temporalContext: The talk was delivered at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 on July 1, 2026, and the video was published on July 24, 2026. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026. On August 13, 2026, approximately three weeks after the video was published, Dynatrace announced a definitive agreement to acquire Arize AI for $915M, meaning the corporate context surrounding Arize's products (AX, Signal, Phoenix, OpenInference) changed significantly shortly after the talk was recorded. The Signal product blog post was published July 29, 2026, five days after the video, and the first-party Signal tutorial was published August 4, 2026.

concepts.name: Agent-consumed observability
concepts.explanation: Observability is shifting from human-facing dashboards (UIs, graphs) to telemetry that coding agents read to diagnose and fix software autonomously. Traces tell agents what code path software actually took, eliminating the need to guess among millions of paths.
concepts.importance: The foundational thesis that redefines the purpose and consumers of observability infrastructure for the age of autonomous agents.

concepts.name: Self-improving agent systems
concepts.explanation: Agents that autonomously investigate production errors, propose fixes, and create evaluators for recurring failures so the system catches them automatically next time, forming a continuous improvement loop.
concepts.importance: Represents the vision of systems that get better every time they fail, moving from human-driven to autonomous improvement.

concepts.name: Online evaluations (LLM-as-a-judge)
concepts.explanation: AI-judged assessments layered onto production traces, running periodically or at full scale across datasets. Evaluators can be created for recurring failure patterns like prompt injection.
concepts.importance: Enables scalable, automated quality assessment of agent behavior in production without manual review of every trace.

concepts.name: Automated evaluator creation for recurring failures
concepts.explanation: When a failure pattern recurs, users can create evaluators that automatically detect that pattern in future production traces, closing the loop between one-time investigation and persistent prevention.
concepts.importance: Transforms one-time investigations into persistent automated guardrails, making the system progressively smarter.

concepts.name: Coding agent harness integration
concepts.explanation: Using coding agents like Claude Code as the fix-generation harness within an observability-driven workflow, where the harness reads filesystem traces and proposes code changes or pull requests.
concepts.importance: Bridges observability data and code generation, making autonomous remediation possible through existing developer tooling.

concepts.name: OpenInference semantic conventions for AI tracing
concepts.explanation: An open standard built on OpenTelemetry that defines span kinds (LLM, Tool, Agent, Retriever) and semantic conventions making AI traces machine-readable for agent-driven debugging. Maintained by Arize with 30+ integrations.
concepts.importance: Provides the standardized trace format that enables agents to reliably parse and reason about production telemetry across platforms.

concepts.name: 10x tracing and logging for agent enablement
concepts.explanation: Teams should trace and log ten times more than current levels because that telemetry reveals the exact code path software took, enabling agents to produce real fixes rather than guessing among millions of possible paths.
concepts.importance: Quantitative guidance that redefines observability investment levels for the age of agent-driven debugging.

concepts.name: Confidence as the bottleneck in autonomous fixing
concepts.explanation: The bottleneck has shifted from generating the fix to having confidence that the fix is correct before pushing it to production. You can build at agent speed but cannot yet improve systems at agent speed.
concepts.importance: Identifies the true constraint in agent-driven software improvement and motivates the evidence-gathering approach over raw fix generation.

concepts.name: Inverted debugging loop
concepts.explanation: Instead of a human grabbing a ticket and investigating an error, the agent pre-investigates issues and creates evidence-backed GitHub issues before a human reviews them. This shifts the human role from responder to reviewer.
concepts.importance: Core architectural pattern that defines how observability-driven agent automation restructures incident response workflows.

concepts.name: Traces-on-filesystem approach
concepts.explanation: Skills pull production traces and logs down as temp files into the repository alongside code, enabling coding agents like Claude Code to work with real execution evidence rather than dashboard guesses. Trace files can reach 10 megabytes.
concepts.importance: The key technical unlock that bridges observability data and coding agent capabilities; without it, agents cannot reason about production failures.

concepts.name: Composable skills for observability
concepts.explanation: Modular, reusable capabilities that find the right traces and format them as files for agent consumption. Simply pointing a coding agent at raw data does not work; the skill surface area must be designed so the agent can work effectively.
concepts.importance: The abstraction layer that makes agent-driven debugging practical; without well-designed skills, coding agents cannot navigate observability data.

concepts.name: Sandboxed agent execution
concepts.explanation: Moving the local debugging experience into sandboxes triggered periodically or by events from observability platforms, enabling autonomous investigation at scale without human initiation.
concepts.importance: Enables agents to run safely and continuously in production environments, transitioning from local developer tools to operational infrastructure.

concepts.name: Evidence-based issue creation
concepts.explanation: The agent creates GitHub issues with attached traces and skills-based evidence, providing humans with a cold start that includes full context for the problem rather than a bare error report.
concepts.importance: Reduces investigation time by pre-gathering evidence and context before human review, making the human review step far more efficient.

concepts.name: VPC deployment for enterprise security
concepts.explanation: Arize installs in customer VPCs because enterprise customers like Uber and Booking will not connect production systems to external model providers such as Anthropic.
concepts.importance: Critical deployment constraint that determines whether observability-driven agent automation can be adopted in regulated or security-conscious environments.

concepts.name: Agent improvement loop
concepts.explanation: The closed loop of investigate, propose, review, ship, and observe again, where production signals feed back into agent prompts, tools, and skills for continuous improvement.
concepts.importance: Defines the end-to-end workflow that makes agents self-improving rather than one-shot fix generators.

concepts.name: Multi-agent swarm management
concepts.explanation: The platform tracks swarms of running agents, supports session viewing, transcript download, and resuming Claude sessions locally for debugging and oversight.
concepts.importance: Essential for operating multiple concurrent agent investigations in production environments at enterprise scale.

sections.title: Arize, Alyx, and why v1 sucked
sections.summary: Lopatecki introduces himself as founder and builder at Arize. Their in-product agent Alyx's first version failed two years ago despite being early to market. Signal is the next-generation automation built from lessons learned.

sections.title: Observability changing: dashboards to agent telemetry
sections.summary: Observability was built for humans clicking graphs. Now it is becoming telemetry that coding agents read to make fixes. Traces tell agents what code path software took; without them agents are guessing among millions of paths. The goal is systems that autonomously fix themselves.

sections.title: The bottleneck is confidence, not the fix
sections.summary: You can build at agent speed but cannot yet improve systems at agent speed. The bottleneck is no longer generating the fix but confidence that the fix is correct before pushing.

sections.title: Inverting the loop: agent investigates first
sections.summary: Instead of humans grabbing tickets and investigating, the agent pre-investigates errors and puts up issues with evidence before a human looks. Humans still drive steps two and three today but move from responder to reviewer. Skills gather context; triggers are periodic or event-based.

sections.title: Traces on filesystem: the key unlock
sections.summary: Skills pull traces and logs down as temp files into the repo alongside the code. This combination of data in file format plus code in the repo is what lets agents produce real fixes. Coding harnesses work well with files but poorly with dashboards.

sections.title: From laptop to sandboxes
sections.summary: People run coding agents locally today. The shift is moving that local debugging experience into sandboxes triggered periodically or by events from observability platforms.

sections.title: Real fix: Alyx stream-canceled bug
sections.summary: A real example where Alyx errored on stream-canceled events. Signal ran in the background, gathered the data, and produced a one-to-two-line fix. Lopatecki notes one-line fixes are ideal and bigger fixes still need a human to spearhead, but the cold start with full evidence is the value.

sections.title: Why you should trace ten times more
sections.summary: Traces and evals do not go away. You should trace and log ten times more because that telemetry reveals the exact code path software took. Previously humans could not dig through excessive logs, but agents can, enabling continuous self-improvement loops.

sections.title: Product demo: Signal, AX, and Phoenix
sections.summary: Arize has AX (SaaS, also deployable in VPC), Phoenix (open source), and Signal (currently in AX). Signal periodically runs, creates GitHub issues with evidence, creates evaluators, and adds findings to datasets. Skills include Google Cloud and logging system integrations.

sections.title: Financial trading agent demo
sections.summary: Demo of a financial trading agent in AX answering stock trading questions. Lopatecki notes he would not recommend building financial trading agents yet. Signal surfaces issues with attached traces and skills-based evidence.

sections.title: Open-box customization: harnesses, sandboxes, and skills
sections.summary: The system is open-box: users pick their harness (e.g., Claude Code), sandbox (Arize, Daytona, or others), prompts, and skills. Customers like Uber and Booking will not connect production systems to external providers, so Arize installs in VPCs. The platform tracks swarms of agents, supports session viewing, transcript download, and resuming Claude sessions locally. Users can add custom skills, link repos, and use pre-baked skills.

sections.title: Q&A: Why not just point Claude Code at your data?
sections.summary: Lopatecki explains that simply pointing Claude Code at data does not work without well-designed skills that find the right traces and format them as files. Files can reach 10 megabytes. Arize provides composable skills including Pyroscope for memory profiling and customer cohorting. The skill surface area must be designed so Claude can work effectively.

sections.title: Q&A: Where do the evals come in?
sections.summary: Online evals are AI-judged assessments layered onto production traces. Skills allow agents to grab eval data from traces. Evals tend to be built for previously seen failures like prompt injection. Users can create evaluators for recurring failures so the system catches them automatically. LLM-as-a-judge can run at scale across full datasets while Signal runs more periodically.

organization.name: Arize AI
organization.summary: Arize AI (Arize AI, Inc.) is an AI engineering and observability platform company headquartered in San Francisco, California. Founded circa 2019-2020 by Jason Lopatecki (CEO) and Aparna Dhinakaran (CPO), the company develops the Arize AX managed platform for observing, evaluating, and improving AI agents and LLM applications, as well as Phoenix, a leading open-source AI observability and evaluation tool, and OpenInference, an open-source semantic convention standard for GenAI observability built on OpenTelemetry. The company has approximately 165 employees, $131M in total funding across 3 rounds, and approximately $13M in annual revenue. Notable customers include Uber, Booking.com, Wayfair, PagerDuty, and TripAdvisor. Key investors include Foundation Capital (seed lead, 2020), Battery Ventures, TCV, Swift Ventures, and Evolution. On August 13, 2026, Dynatrace announced the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire Arize AI for $915M to converge AI observability with software observability. The video was published on July 24, 2026, approximately three weeks before the acquisition announcement.
organization.status: Acquired by Dynatrace. On August 13, 2026, Dynatrace announced the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire Arize AI for $915M ($815M cash plus replacement equity awards). Founders Jason Lopatecki and Aparna Dhinakaran will join Dynatrace. Arize AI operates as part of Dynatrace, combining AI observability with software observability capabilities.

technologies.label: Signal — Agent Automation and Inverted Debugging Loop
technologies.summary: Signal is Arize's next-generation agent automation system that inverts the traditional debugging loop: instead of a human grabbing a ticket and investigating, the agent pre-investigates production errors using composable skills, gathers evidence from traces and logs, and creates issues with attached evidence or proposes fixes before a human reviews. Built from lessons learned when Arize's first agent Alyx failed two years ago, Signal runs periodically or is triggered by events from observability platforms. It demonstrated a real fix for a stream-canceled bug producing a one-to-two-line code change. The system is open-box: users pick their harness (e.g., Claude Code), sandbox, prompts, and skills. Signal also supports online evals—AI-judged assessments layered onto production traces—and can create evaluators for recurring failure patterns to catch them automatically.
technologies.role: Signal is the central product and primary subject of the talk. Lopatecki presents its architecture, demonstrates it in action with a real stream-canceled bug fix, and discusses its product positioning within the AX platform.

technologies.label: OpenInference — AI Tracing Protocol on OpenTelemetry
technologies.summary: OpenInference is an open standard for AI observability tracing maintained by Arize AI, built on top of OpenTelemetry. It defines semantic conventions including span kinds (LLM, Tool, Agent, Retriever) and attributes that make AI application traces machine-readable. This standardization is the technical foundation that enables agents to reliably parse and reason about production telemetry, which is essential for the traces-on-filesystem approach where coding agents consume trace files. OpenInference has 30+ native integrations and is portable to any OpenTelemetry-compatible backend. Lopatecki argues teams should trace and log ten times more than today because that telemetry reveals the exact code path software took, and OpenInference provides the standardized format that makes this telemetry consumable by agents.
technologies.role: Foundational protocol underlying the tracing architecture central to the talk. While not explicitly named in the transcript, it is the open standard maintained by Arize that provides the semantic conventions making traces agent-consumable, as verified through first-party documentation, the GitHub repository, and the specification page.

technologies.label: Phoenix — Open-Source AI Observability Platform
technologies.summary: Phoenix is Arize AI's open-source AI observability platform, built on OpenTelemetry and supporting the OpenInference standard. It provides tracing, evaluation, datasets, experiments, and prompt management as open-source, with a path to the commercial Arize AX platform for managed scale. Phoenix represents the OSS foundation that underlies the observability infrastructure discussed in the talk—the platform where traces are collected, stored, and made available for agents to consume. With approximately 11K GitHub stars, Phoenix has active community adoption. The talk's thesis that observability is shifting from human-facing dashboards to agent-consumed telemetry is embodied in Phoenix's role as the platform that feeds agent-driven debugging workflows.
technologies.role: Mentioned as part of Arize's product lineup (AX, Phoenix, Signal). Phoenix is the OSS offering that provides the tracing and evaluation infrastructure underlying the agent automation system.

technologies.label: Traces-on-Filesystem with Composable Skills — Agent Debugging Technique
technologies.summary: The traces-on-filesystem approach is the key technical unlock described in the talk. Composable skills pull production traces and logs down as temp files directly into the code repository alongside the source code. This combination of data in file format plus code in the repo is what lets coding agents like Claude Code produce real fixes rather than guesses—because coding harnesses work well with files but poorly with dashboards. Trace files can reach 10 megabytes in size. The skill surface area must be deliberately designed so the agent can find the right traces and format them effectively; simply pointing Claude Code at raw data does not work. Arize provides pre-baked skills including Pyroscope for memory profiling and customer cohorting, and users can add custom skills. The technique also depends on sandboxed execution environments where agents run triggered periodically or by events.
technologies.role: Described as the key technical innovation that makes agent-driven debugging practical. Lopatecki dedicates a full section to explaining why this approach works and why simply pointing Claude Code at dashboards does not.

entities.name: Jason Lopatecki
entities.relation: Speaker and presenter of the talk. Co-Founder and CEO of Arize AI. Previously co-founder and Chief Innovation Officer at TubeMogul (IPO, then acquired by Adobe). UC Berkeley EECS graduate.

entities.name: Aparna Dhinakaran
entities.relation: Co-author of the accompanying Signal blog post and co-founder/CPO of Arize AI. Previously built ML infrastructure at Uber. Co-presented the Arize Observe 2026 keynote that frames the architecture discussed in this talk.

entities.name: Arize AI
entities.relation: The company whose products (Arize AX, Signal, Phoenix, OpenInference) are the subject of the talk. Founded 2020 by Jason Lopatecki and Aparna Dhinakaran.

entities.name: Arize AX
entities.relation: The managed AI engineering platform that hosts Signal, Managed Agents, Agent Studio, and the agent improvement loop described in the talk. Available as SaaS or VPC.

entities.name: Signal
entities.relation: The central product launched/demonstrated in the talk. A managed agent that continuously reviews production traces, surfaces ranked issues with evidence and proposed fixes, and can open pull requests via Managed Agents.

entities.name: Phoenix
entities.relation: Arize's open-source AI observability platform, the OSS foundation underlying Arize AX. Provides tracing, evaluation, datasets, experiments, and prompt management. ~11K GitHub stars.

entities.name: Alyx
entities.relation: The AI engineering agent built into Arize AX that Arize dogfooded before shipping Signal to customers. Referenced in the talk as the team's own agent that 'frankly sucked' initially.

entities.name: Managed Agents
entities.relation: Enterprise feature in Arize AX that carries Signal investigations into the codebase to propose fixes and open pull requests. Available to Enterprise customers in beta at time of talk.

entities.name: Agent Studio
entities.relation: Configurable agent workflow tool in Arize AX with templates for investigating traces, triaging alerts, analyzing costs, and proposing PRs. Mentioned in the talk as part of the managed agent workflow.

entities.name: OpenInference
entities.relation: Open standard for AI observability tracing maintained by Arize, built on OpenTelemetry. Provides the semantic conventions (span kinds, attributes) that make traces machine-readable for agent-driven debugging as described in the talk.

entities.name: OpenTelemetry
entities.relation: Industry-standard telemetry framework that OpenInference is built on. Provides the transport and span/trace primitives underlying the observability architecture discussed in the talk.

evidence.excerpt: you're going to trace 10 times more. You're going to log 10 times more because that helps you know what path your software took
evidence.supports: Teams should trace and log 10x more to enable agents to know exact code paths

evidence.excerpt: we've kind of inverted this this loop which is like a human you know looks at things and an agent uh fixes it to a person now can wake up with with an idea of the issues
evidence.supports: Arize inverts the debugging loop so the agent investigates before the human

evidence.excerpt: This was uh a kind of one or two line fix that it comes up with. These are these are ideal but a lot of times the fixes are bigger
evidence.supports: One-to-two-line fixes are the easy case; bigger fixes need human involvement

evidence.excerpt: observability used to be for humans. Used to be a UI you click, a graph you click
evidence.supports: Observability is shifting from human-facing dashboards to agent-consumed telemetry

evidence.supports: Customers require VPC deployment because they will not connect production systems to external model providers

evidence.excerpt: in some cases we have 10meg files like sitting in the repo
evidence.supports: Trace files pulled into the repo can reach 10 megabytes in size
